memoryText: Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Luke 15:7 slowly, several times, and say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jesus says this at the end of the parable of the lost sheep, to Pharisees who complained that he welcomed sinners and ate with them. It is his answer to their grumbling and a window into the heart of heaven.

“Just so.” The shepherd’s joy over the found sheep is a picture of heaven’s joy. Jesus is not describing an anxious God who tolerates repentant sinners. He is describing a God who celebrates.

“More joy in heaven.” Heaven is not a quiet place. It rejoices. When a single person turns from sin and trusts in God, the angels rejoice and the Father himself is glad. Your repentance was a reason for celebration in heaven.

“One sinner who repents.” One, not a crowd. Each person matters to God. The shepherd left ninety-nine to seek one. Repentance here means a change of mind and direction, turning from self and sin to God.

“Ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.” Jesus says this with irony, for the Pharisees thought they were righteous. In truth, everyone needs to repent. The only people who miss the party are those who think they do not need it.

If you have ever felt that God is disappointed in you, say this verse. When you come home, he runs to meet you.
weekInReview: This week you prayed Psalm 27 and its bold trust, “Whom shall I fear?”, and Psalm 28, which moves from a cry to praise. Psalm 31:1-18 gave you the prayer “Into your hand I commit my spirit,” and “My times are in your hand.” In Luke 13 to 19 you heard Jesus warn about the narrow door and tell the stories of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son, in which a father runs to meet a returning child. You listened to his hard words about money, the rich man and Lazarus, the ten lepers, and the coming of the kingdom. You saw a widow persist in prayer, a tax collector go home justified, a blind man receive his sight, and Zacchaeus climb down from a tree. You read the verse that sums up the Gospel: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
reflectionQuestions: In the parable of the lost son, the father runs to meet the returning child. What does this tell you about how God receives you when you come back to him?
Jesus said he came to seek and to save the lost (19:10). How does his seeking of Zacchaeus, and of you, show who Jesus is?
The tax collector prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Where do you need to stop justifying yourself and simply ask for mercy?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents.
Thank him for seeking you and bringing you home.
Ask him to keep you from the elder brother’s spirit.
